newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Republicans used Hong Kong money, panel hears.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Republicans used Hong Kong money, panel hears.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

A Hong Kong businessman gave a $2.1 million loan guarantee to a Republican think-tank, which passed on the money to the Republican Party and later defaulted on the debt, a U.S. Senate committee was told on Wednesday.

Florida lawyer Benton Becker, a one-time legal counsel to former President Gerald Ford, laid out the story to the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, which is investigating illegal foreign involvement in the 1996 elections.
Becker represents Hong Kong businessman Ambrose Young, who made at least $122,000 in illegal contributions to the Republican Party. The money was returned in May.
The party also disclosed on Wednesday that it had returned another $20,000 to Young on June 20, 1997.

This was the first opportunity for Democrats on the committee to focus on possible Republican violations after two weeks of testimony that dealt exclusively with alleged illegal or improper behaviour by the Democrats.
The committee, in a rare moment of bipartisan cooperation, voted to grant immunity from prosecution to four Buddhist nuns and one other person, rejecting Justice Department opposition.

All but one Democrat on the committee sided with the Republican majority in voting 15-1 to give immunity to the nuns, who were involved in a questionable fund-raising event last year attended by Vice President Al Gore.

At the April 1996 event at the Hsi Lai Temple in Hacienda Heights in California, nuns who took a vow of poverty wrote $5,000 checks to the Democratic National Committee and were reimbursed one day later.

The committee voted 13-3 to grant immunity to Keshi Zhan, a $22,000-a-year-employee of the welfare department in Arlington, Virginia, who gave $15,000 to the Democratic Party last year -- money the committee suspects she received from Yah Lin Trie, a former Little Rock restaurant owner and friend of President Bill Clinton who has fled the country.

A congressman involved in the probe of campaign finance abuses made public a letter on Wednesday informing him that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was taking a personal interest in locating and questioning Trie.

Representative Gerald Solomon of New York, Chairman of the House Rules Committee, released a letter from an assistant secretary of state which said: "We informed the Chinese government that this is a high priority in which Secretary Albright is personally interested."
Solomon commended Albright, saying she was rising "head and shoulders above the partisan politics" surrounding the probe. He said Trie was "one of the principle subjects" of the investigation.
Becker's testimony centred on the relationship between Ambrose Young and former Republican Party chairman Haley Barbour, who will testify to the committee on Thursday.

In 1994, Barbour persuaded Young to grant a $2.1 million loan guarantee to the National Policy Forum, a Republican think-tank. "I have since learned that almost immediately the NPF transferred $1.6 million to the RNC (Republican National Committee)," Becker said.

Democrats say the RNC sent that money in the final days of the 1994 election to candidates in close races, helping them to an electoral triumph in which the party won control of both houses of Congress and most large state governorships.
They will try to build a case that Barbour knowingly solicited the funds for the election and used the think-tank as a smoke screen.

Democrats distributed a September 1994 letter from Young to Barbour in which the Hong Kong businessman said: "We are willing to consider the support of $2.1 million, which is the amount you have expressed to me that is urgently needed and directly related to the November election."
Republicans say this was used to pay off a debt from the think-tank to the RNC that had sapped party resources.
Barbour later urged Young to write off the loan but Young refused. However, in April 1996, the NPF defaulted on the loan and Young lost his money.
